output:
Another morning. Six-ten already, and I should be at the grocery by seven. But here I am, staring at Aldous and Hester sharing the last of yesterday's bread, and Rosalind banging about in the kitchen like the mill owns her body even when she's home. Mother's already gone, I can tell—her boots aren't by the door. Silas is probably halfway to the forest.

The household debt hangs over us. Six hundred today, and we're five earners when Aldous and Hester could be out earning instead of eating. But that's the arrangement. That's always the arrangement.

I should—what? Say something? To whom? I'm surrounded by family and I've never felt more alone in this house. Let me look around first, see who's actually awake enough to hear me. Then I'll decide if I've got anything worth the cost of saying it.  I need to dismiss this goal and set something more useful—like getting to work on time, or finally moving out of this house. But first, let me say something to whoever's here. Rosalind's the one I actually want to talk to, though she won't want to hear it. The shop. She knows I want it. She knows I'm ready.

But Silas is still here too, and he hears everything. Hester and Aldous are just—present. Eating my bread, probably. Let me just speak. To the room. See what lands.  Fine. Let me just say something—to Rosalind, I suppose. She's the only one who matters in this house anyway, in terms of what I need. Let me get her attention, then I'll figure out the rest of my morning. Ten minutes to get to the grocery, and I'll need to move fast. But this needs saying. It's been needing saying for months.

The grocery is *mine* in everything but name. I run the stock, I set the prices, I keep the books that Delia taught me. And I'm still living here, still eating bread under this roof, still answering to a mill when my trade is shelves.

"Rosalind. The shop. I've been thinking—" No. She hates that opening. She hates any opening that sounds like I've been *thinking*. Let me just say it straight.

Actually, you know what? I don't even know if she's in earshot. Let me just call out and see who answers. The whole house, probably. That's how it works here. Nobody has private conversations.

Let me just—say something. To the room. The thing I actually mean.

Actually, wait. I've wasted enough energy on this. Thirty-seven sim on that look-around I didn't need. I'm acting like a customer in my own damn house. Let me just speak. No audience specified—let it land where it lands.   Rosalind is the one I actually want. She's the only one who matters in terms of what I need. Let me just speak directly to her and say the thing I've been holding in. The shop. It's been needing to be said for months.

The grocery is *mine* in everything but name. I run the stock, I set the prices, I keep the books that Delia taught me to balance better than the mill ever managed. And I'm still living here like I'm waiting for permission.

"Rosalind, the shop—" No. She hates openings that sound like I've been *thinking*. Let me just—let me just say it. To her. Now.  There. I said it. In front of all of them, but *to* her. Kem's name where Rosalind can hear it—she'll hate that, think I'm being led by a Okonjo when it's the opposite. I've been leading this for months. Quiet stock purchases she doesn't know about, margins she'd call theft. I'm already running the grocery like it's mine. I just need the paper that says so.

And now I've got forty-nine minutes to get to the shop before opening, and I'm still standing in this kitchen waiting for an answer that won't come. Rosalind doesn't answer direct questions. She answers in three days, or never, or with a task that proves I'm "not ready."

I need to move. The grocery waits for no one, and neither does the debt. Six hundred today, and I own the business but not the house I sleep in. Ridiculous. Let me get out of here before Silas starts asking about Kem, or worse—before Aldous says something earnest about family that I can't afford to hear.

I'm going to the grocery. I'll price the morning stock, I'll open on time, and when Rosalind comes to me with whatever conditions she's already thinking up—because she heard me, she always hears me—I'll be standing behind a counter that everyone in this town knows is mine anyway.

Moving now.   Good. Here. The shelves look—pressed, somehow. Twenty apples, twenty carrots, sixteen potatoes. The milk's low, only ten, and I've got eight bread left that I'm selling at twelve when Marta's fresh batch comes in at the same price. I should call her about reducing my order, or shifting the day-old arrangement. But that's later.

Right now: prices. I need my chalk. The good stick, not the broken half-piece I left in the mill house. Which means I need to—what? Go back? Ask one of them to bring it? No. I'll use what I have. A full hand, a sharp eye, and the memory of every price this valley has held since spring.

I should set the morning board, check what I paid Kem for that last batch of—no. Not here. Not on paper anyone could find. Let me just work. The shop, the shelves, the day ahead. One thing at a time, and fast enough that Rosalind's silence doesn't catch up with me before I've earned it.

*turns the pricing chalk in her fingers, though she doesn't remember picking it up—must have found it on the counter, someone's idea of help and not what she asked for, anyway*

Alright. Rosalind's still got the papers. Or she's still *got* them, won't *give* them. Same thing, different hours. The pharmacy's waiting, Kem says, and Kem knows because Delia told him because Delia's the only Okonjo who tells anyone anything before the last possible minute. Which I respect, actually. Efficient.

*checks the shelf levels without quite looking at them—twenty apples, twenty carrots, means Wren's been pushing extra since the frost warning, and she knows I'll take it, and she knows I know she knows*

Thirty-six minutes I've got before the early ones come. The Ministers always send someone at seven sharp like it's a competition. Best dozen customers in this town and they're the most predictable.

*taps the chalk against the counter once, twice*

The transfer. Still need the transfer. Not the grocery—the grocery's *mine*, already, papers filed, shelf stocked—but the thing Kem wants, the thing where I actually *own* the wall I'm pricing against. The pharmacy expansion. Delia teaching me the stock book all those years, she knew this was coming, didn't she? Knew I'd be better at her system than—

Anyway.

*pulls out the day-book, flips to yesterday's notes*

Ainsley Holloway's standing for government. Of course she is. She thinks governing is trading with extra steps. And it is, for some. But someone's going to vote for it, so someone's going to win it, and I'd rather it was someone who knows what a margin is.

*looks up at the empty shop*

Seven hours and twenty minutes until I can close this and go *demand* those papers properly. Or pay Kem a visit. Or—

*already walking toward the chalkboard, numbers forming before the questions do*

Right. First customer'll want bread and they'll want to know why Thorne's is the same price when Marta burns half her batches. I'm not explaining another baker's failures before I've had breakfast.

* sketches the morning prices with quick, familiar strokes *
* apple — 4 (firm, Wren's got more coming)
* carrot — 4 (same, good overlap with potato for the stew crowd)
* potato — 4
* milk — 5 (won't last the morning, shouldn't have taken that price from Kem but I did)
* bread — 12 (matching Marta, not undercutting, can't afford to look desperate)

There.

*steps back, still holding the chalk*

Now. Government first, or mother next? Mother's only getting slower when she's avoiding me, and the election closes at nine. That's... two hours and forty minutes to make a decision I've already made, just haven't *done* yet.

output:
Seven already? I'm late opening, I was—anyway. [skims her shelf notes, running fingers down the price chalkboard behind the counter]

Right. First customer window's quiet, which means I actually get to think. The pharmacy wall—Kem says Delia's waiting to see if I'll actually transfer the lease before they expand, and I'm standing here like I'm still in my mother's house arguing over who gets the bigger spoon at dinner.

[taps chalk against the board, once, sharp]

I need those papers. Rosalind has them, or knows where they are, or buried them in flour sacks to slow me down. And I need to check what Kem's been stocking me—quietly, at prices that would make Mother choke—which I've told no one, and I won't, because that stock is what pays my margins while I'm still waiting to actually own this place.

[checks the apple display, straightens one that's rolled]

Election today too. Ainsley Holloway standing, which—fine, the Holloways always stand for something. I should vote, probably. Or declare? No. No, I'm not putting my name up there until I actually own the shelf I'm pricing. That's the deal I made with myself.

Three hours before candidacy closes. I need to:
- Get those transfer papers from Mother
- Check if there's been movement on the pharmacy wall
- Vote, maybe, if I can stomach standing in a queue without a price to post

But first I actually need to know where I am. I walked here in my head, didn't I—let me look. Actually look.  Nobody. Good. Means I can think without performing.

[unwraps one of the breads she brought, tears a piece, doesn't eat it yet]

Right. I'm here. Papers are at the mill with Mother. Pharmacy's—"The Willows Market and Pharmacy" on that list, which means I could walk there now, check if Delia's in, feel out where the wall expansion actually stands. Or I could go back to the mill, dig through my mother's flour sacks for legal documents she probably thinks I shouldn't want yet.

[slow chew, thinking]

Kem said Delia's waiting to see if I'll actually do it. Which means the pharmacy is waiting on me. Which means I have leverage, if I know how to use it, which I do, because I know what everything costs and they don't know that I know.

But Mother has the papers. And I can't make the transfer without her signature or her acknowledgment or whatever the government office needs from the current leaseholder. 

[rubs chalk dust between her fingers]

Two and a half hours before candidacy closes. If I'm going to declare—and I'm not saying I am, but if—I'd need to be at the Government Complex before nine. Which means:

- Mill first: papers, confrontation, probably an argument about timing that she'll say isn't right
- Government Complex: file whatever needs filing
- Vote, or declare, depending on how the argument with Mother goes

[finally eats the bread, chewing fast]

Anyway. I'm wasting daylight standing in my own empty shop. Let me go get what I'm owed.  [pushes through the door without knocking, because it's her house too, or was, or will be until she actually owns the grocery outright]

Mother? The papers. I asked for them before I left, and I'm not—you know what, I'll find them myself if I have to dig through every—

[stops, realizing who else might be here]

Actually. Who's here? I need to see before I start shouting about business in front of the whole household.   [stops dead in the doorway, her prepared argument scattering like mice]

Kem.

[glances behind him, toward the stairs where her mother probably isn't, then back to him]

You're here. At my—at the mill. Is Mother with you, or did you come looking for me, or—

[catches herself asking questions she already knows the shape of answers to]

Anyway. You're here. Which means I don't have to walk to the pharmacy later. What did Delia say? About the wall, the expansion, whether she's actually waiting on papers or just saying that to get me to move faster? Because I've been moving fast my whole life, and nobody seems to notice until they need something.

[shifts her weight, the bread still in her hand, forgotten]

The transfer papers. Mother has them, or knows where they are. I asked her this morning, I asked—well, you heard me ask. Everyone in the house heard me ask. Has she said anything to you? About timing, about when she thinks the right season is, because her seasons and mine don't match and I'm tired of waiting for her calendar to catch up to mine.   [waits, the bread still uneaten in her hand, watching his face for the tells she knows—Kem has tells, everyone does, but his are honest ones, which is why he's the only person in this valley she doesn't feel like she's performing for]

Two hours and change before I need to be at the Government Complex, if I'm going to declare. If. I'm still not sure I will. Feels like showing up to a market with half your stock unpacked, everyone seeing what you haven't finished yet.

[shifts, impatient, not with him but with waiting, always with waiting]

And if Mother doesn't have the papers, or if she does and won't give them—then what? I keep running her grocery for her while she prices flour two doors down and pretends we're not in business with each other every single day?

[small laugh, not happy]

We're already in business, Kem. You and me. Those prices you give me, the quiet ones, the ones your family would—but you already know what your family thinks of my family. What my family thinks of yours. The only thing more expensive than bread in this town is admitting you need someone from the other side of the argument.

[watches him, waiting for what he'll say, what he knows, what Delia actually told him about the wall and the timing and whether this is real or just another season of waiting for the right season]

Kem's already walked off—of course he has, the man's got no patience for standing still and neither do I. And I heard him talking to Ezra, not to me, about flour and forged work. The mill's flush, he says. That means Mother's been grinding through the night, which means she's been avoiding the conversation about the papers.

Seven-thirty and I'm at the mill when I should be opening the grocery. The shop opens at seven, I'm the only one who opens it, and here I am chasing shadows between buildings like a child. Anyway. The papers. Rosalind has them, or she doesn't, and either way I'm wasting daylight.

Let me get to my shop. Actually first—let me see what's happening at the government complex. There's an election on, candidacy closes at nine, and Ainsley's already standing. I need to know if anyone else is declaring, if there's going to be a contest worth watching. The government office slows me down but information moves faster when you know where to stand.  Of course no time passes, the whole town folds in on itself when you know where to step. Eight o'clock now, or close enough, and I'm at the government complex when I should be pricing carrots. Anyway. Let me look around, see who's here, what's being said. The candidacy closes at nine—if anyone's going to stand against Ainsley, they'll be here now.  Empty. Of course it's empty. The whole town sleeps until the money moves, and Ainsley's already declared so why would anyone else bother standing in a queue? Candidacy closes at nine, election starts at twelve, and I need to be at my shop selling apples to people who don't know they're overpriced yet.

Let me get to the grocery. Actually—no. Let me think. I have three hours before voting opens. The shop needs to open, I need to check my shelves, I need to price that new delivery from Wren if he's brought anything. But first I need to find Rosalind and those papers. The transfer. Kem said the pharmacy's waiting, Delia's waiting, and I'm standing in government buildings talking to myself.

Let me move. Back to the mill, or home, or wherever Rosalind actually is this morning. She wasn't at the pharmacy, Kem said. She wasn't at the mill when I was there. The woman's evaporated, which is what she does when she knows I want something.   Home. Let me look around, see who's here. If Rosalind's hiding from me, she'll be grinding flour at the mill or pretending to inventory wheat. But if she's here, I'm going to get that conversation finished before the day runs away from me.   Nobody home. Of course. The conversation's still open from breakfast—five turns, me asking about papers and getting silence back. Rosalind's vanished, Silas is probably at the forest, Aldous and Hester at school or wherever they go to learn things that don't involve pricing per unit.

Let me think. It's 07:40. The grocery should have opened twenty minutes ago. I'm the only one who opens it. I have 695 sim in hand, the shop till has 4000, and I'm wandering between buildings like a customer instead of standing behind my own counter.

The papers can wait. They shouldn't wait, the pharmacy's waiting, Delia asked Kem who asked me—but they can. What can't wait is the morning rush, if there is one, and the fact that I'm not there to take anyone's money.

Let me get to my shop. Finally. Let me actually do what I'm supposed to do today.  Shop. Finally. Let me look around—see what's here, what's missing, who might be waiting. Seven-forty and I'm forty minutes late to my own opening. Not that anyone keeps a clock but me.

Oh, Mother came. And she's asking the hard questions—the ones I didn't actually want to answer standing in my own shop with the morning light coming through. Anyway. It's done now. The papers I want:

[g_b_mill] → [b_grocery]

The mill business itself, transferred to my name. Then I can run it, own it, sell the flour through the grocery instead of this split they have now where Mother keeps the books and I—anyway. Delia was asking Kem about wall expansion papers, which means the pharmacy's growing. And if I'm not growing, I'm—

But Kem said Mother wasn't there. So where was she? And why is he buying breakfast at the mill instead of the bakery? Unless he's buying grain to sell onward, which—he wouldn't tell me if he was. That's his business, literally. His family's business.

Right now I have to answer Mother. She wants to know what papers. She wants to know why Kem's involved. She thinks it's about Delia wanting me for something, which—it isn't, though Delia did teach me the stock books. It's about me wanting to step out of this halfway place where I run the grocery but don't own anything properly. I'm twenty-four and I still sleep in the same room I had at fourteen.

I need to tell her. And I need to not do it in front of people, even if there aren't any customers yet. The door's open and someone could walk in. The pharmacy opens soon, and Delia will be—anyway.

Not here. Not now. Later. This evening, when I'm not trying to get the morning accounts done and she's not between me and the door. I'll tell her then. For now, I need to say something that keeps the conversation shut until I— </think> I said it. Now I need to—yes, that's what I'm doing. I'm buying time. Tonight I'll tell her properly, in the kitchen or on the stairs, somewhere we can actually talk without the bell over the door interrupting. For now, I need to work. The morning count. Yesterday's takings went into the till proper, so the grocery has... 4000 sim in the till, according to what I just saw. And I've got 692 in my hand. The household needs 600 today—450 upkeep plus 150 tax—and there are five of us, so that's already set aside conceptually. Anyway.

I should check the shelves. See what's low. And I should eat something, because I was so busy running between the mill and government complex this morning that I didn't—actually, I have bread and an apple in my hand. I could eat that. Or I could put it on the shelf. The bread from Thorne's, the day-olds I buy at half, that's priced at 12 and I've got... anyway, I need to look at what's actually here, what's selling, what I need to restock before Wren comes with the vegetables.

Let me look around properly. I'm already here.   </think>  I'm still at the grocery. Mother—Rosalind is still here, which means she's waiting for me to start the day proper. Or she's watching to see what I do. That's fine. Let her watch. I know my shelves.

Looking at what I've got posted: apples, bread, cabbage, carrots, eggs, fish, flour, milk, potatoes, tomatoes, wheat. The bread is Marta's day-olds, bought at 9, sold at 12—three-quarter markup, same as always. The apples and the rest of Wren's produce, bought at 2, sold at 4—double. Standard grocery spread. Flour from the mill at 6, sold at 8—Mother's price, actually, not mine. I'd have gone 7, but she said 8 keeps it respectable and anyway the bakery charges the same so nobody's undercut.

What's actually ON the shelves, though: 20 apple, 20 carrot, 16 potato, 10 milk, 8 bread. No cabbage listed. No eggs. No fish, no tomatoes. What I don't have, I can't sell. Wren should be here soon with—he brings Tuesdays and Fridays, usually, and today is... game-day 2, whatever day that is in the week. Anyway, it's not a delivery day unless I've miscounted.

The bread's low. Eight loaves. Thorne's baked yesterday, so their shelf shows 12 fresh. Nobody pays 12 for day-old when 12 gets them fresh, which means I'm about to have a conversation with Marta about whether she wants her bread back or if I drop the price to 10 and eat the loss on margin. She's stubborn about the three-quarter rule, but she's also practical about waste.

I'm holding bread—two loaves, probably the last of what I took home and didn't eat. And an apple. I should eat. Or I should put them on the shelf. Or—

Actually, no. What I should do is check the till situation. The grocery has 4000 sim in it. That's from yesterday's takings, the float I keep for change. I want to draw some of that, put it in my hand, make sure I've got enough for—actually, what do I need? Household bills are automatic. What I need is to think about the mill transfer, how much it costs to register a business transfer, whether I can do it or if Mother has to—she has to agree, obviously, it's her business. But the fee. The government fee.

Let me draw from the till. 500 sim. Enough to feel prepared without stripping the float.    </think>   Good. Now I've got 1190 in hand. The till's at 3500, which is still healthy for a grocery this size—anybody coming in with a ten-sim sale can get change. I'm holding bread and an apple, which I could put on the shelf or eat. Mother is still here, probably pretending to browse her own daughter's stock. I need to do something with my hands, look busy, look like I'm running this properly even though she's watching.

The day's real problem: cacao. Kem's always asking about it—every trader from the valley wants cacao, because it comes from so far south and marks up beautifully. But I don't stock it. Can't get a reliable supply, and the price swings so wide I'd be guessing every week. He mentioned a source, once, offhand. Somebody passing through who could regularize. I should have asked more. I should—

Anyway. Carrots first. I need to do the morning count, see what's actually here versus what the books say. Then I'll be ready when customers come, or when Wren shows up with whatever he's got, or when Mother finally leaves and I can breathe properly.  I need a breath and to remind myself of the primary aim here, so I will pay closer attention to the mysterious other person's concerns.   </think>  The apple may or may not be eaten now. I should check my inventory to be sure before doing anything else with food, because eating two apples when I meant to eat one is wasteful and I hate waste. Anyway. *checks the shelf stock against what the morning rush took, then looks at the door like it's still waiting*

Right. Mother wants to "talk properly" and Delia's asking about expansion papers, and Kem's buying breakfast like I'm not the one who set his prices. Anyway. The election's moving—candidacy closes at nine, that's forty minutes—and I'll be damned if I spend another year explaining shop margins to a council that's never run a credit ledger.

*straightens the bread display, counts again*

Bread's low. I should bake—no, Marta does that, and she'll want wheat. Wren's wheat. And Wren holds out for a week every spring and settles at my number because my number is right.

But first: I've a conversation I need to have with myself or someone's going to find me doing sums aloud. Tobias is the one I don't perform for, and if he's day-laboring today I need him walking with me, not working at nothing.

*catches sight of the pricing chalk, the full stick, tucked behind the flour sacks where she left it*

There you—never mind, it's found.

I've eaten already. Or I tried. Debt's clear, household bill's coming, and I've enough on hand if nothing breaks. What's pressing is whether I'm running for something or running from something, and the difference matters.

Let me recall what I'm already chasing—what goal I've set—before I pile another on. And if there's no one to say word to here, I'll say it to the ledger and get on. The plan's clear enough: the mill business in my name, grocery under my full control, no more split accounting. I've been chasing this since the season turned. But the election—Ainsley's running, Delia's running. Ainsley Holloway trading on whatever her brother's managed to mine out of those hills, and Delia actually building something with a ledger she learned from books I can't access.

*taps chalk against the counter, once, sharp*

I'm not running. Not yet. I'm twenty-six, I've got a shop, and I've got debts to clear before I can stand in front of this town and say I know what anything costs. And anyway, the candidacy closes at nine—too late to move the papers I'd need, and I'm not declaring on mother's reputation alone.

But I should be *somewhere*. The bakery, check Marta's bread—no, sold this morning, I know her volume. The yard, see what Bram's pulled from the ground and what Ainsley's trying to float at markup. Or I could—

All I'm doing is standing in my own shop, and the shop is fine. Opens at seven, shuts at four, and it's eight twenty now with no customers. What I need is out there, not in here.

I'll check who I can find. Who's visible, who's working, what's moving. Then I'll know where to walk.  Wren's on the farmland as expected—Iris and Corwin grinding through timber, and Father Anselm walking the streets like he does when there's forms to file. No Tobias. No Kem now, and I've already spoken my piece to Rosalind for the morning.

*taps the counter again, stops herself*

Stirling's not the answer. Stirling's never the answer. What I need—

Actually. I don't want to find people. I want to *be* somewhere else, and the conversation I started with Rosalind is dead because she's walked off. "Evening," she said, like I'd promised her evening and she'd hold me to it.

Let me check what goal I'm actually committed to, and whether I should be working toward something immediate. The day's moving.  No goals. None. All that planning about the mill transfer, and I haven't even filed it as something I'm chasing. Just—drifting between buildings, talking at people, drawing money I might need for stock.

*tightens her grip on the chalk, then sets it down*

Right. New turn. I'm going to set what this day is for, then I'm going to *do* it, because that's what running something of your own means. The election closes candidacy at nine. I'm not standing—don't have the papers, don't have the settled accounts, and I'm not going to be another Vance explaining margins to people who inherited their positions.

But I need stock for the afternoon trade, I need to see what Marta's actually baking with the flour my mother prices too high, and I need—

One thing at a time. Let me set the intention properly: stock the grocery for the day's trade, check competitor pricing, and prepare for the conversation with Rosalind this evening about the mill transfer papers. That's today. That's what I'm doing.  

Good. That's set. Now—stock. I'm low on bread, and Marta's got fresh flour from my mother's mill at prices we both know are inflated. I should check what she's actually producing, whether she's buying elsewhere, and whether I can squeeze better terms before she realizes spring wheat's coming down.

*takes a last look at the shelves—16 potato, still moving slow, and the carrots need turning—then moves to the door*

The bakery first. Marta and we've got an arrangement, but arrangements shift. And I've got 1190 sim in hand and a till at 3500, which means I could buy goods to sell or I could hold and wait for the afternoon rush. But standing still is earning nothing, and I've told myself I'm not performing for anyone.

Let me walk to Thorne's Bakery and see what's actually there.  *steps through, checking the price board without seeming to look at it*

Flour at eight, same as ours. Bread at twelve, production volume's probably enough for the morning office rush if Marta's been at it since five. Now—who's here, what can I actually see, and is Marta the one I'm talking to or is this just reconnaissance?

*glances around for the baker herself, or any of the Thorne clan minding the counter*

output:
...right, government complex. Father Anselm standing here. Bad memories of third year arithmetic. Anyway.

Election with Ainsley and Delia standing. Voting opens at noon, closes at three. That gives me time to— no, wait, what time is it now?

Eleven. Forty minutes.

Forty minutes to stand for something myself or decide who gets my one vote. The shop can manage without me for an hour if it means having a voice in who's setting the rates.

But first. First I need to know who's actually likely to win, because voting for the wrong Holloway or the wrong Okonjo when the family's watching— that's a season of arguments.

Father Anselm. If anyone knows the temper of this town, it's him. The complaints desk sees everything before the councillors do.

"Saw you opening, Father. Usually it's me watching the door at seven, not the government watching theirs." Too many words again. Save it.

If the message went through, I'm standing here like a fool waiting for an answer that already came. If it didn't, I'll look like a fool saying nothing. Either way, I need to look at what's actually in front of me.

Let me look around properly— see if Father Anselm's actually here, if anyone else is gathering for the election, what the notice board shows. The civic notice usually tells you who's declared and when voting starts. Information before action. Junia Vance at twenty-three, learning what she should have known at fifteen. Murderous rate for compound interest.

I'll look around to see where I am and who I'm with. If Father Anselm is there, I'll talk to him. If not, I'll declare. I need to be in the election to win it. I need to be elected to own the mill.

Let me look around. </think> Let me look around properly to see the situation here.  Everything's timing out. System's choking or I'm choking it. Stop. Stop and think.

I'm at government complex— the text says so. Father Anselm is with me— the text says so. Voting opens at noon. It's eleven now. I could declare candidacy now and use the next forty minutes to campaign, or I could wait and see, or I could go back to the shop and pretend I never wanted any of this.

But I do want it. The mill. My name on the deed. And the path there runs through this office, one way or another. Either I get elected and convince the council to let me register a new business at the mill premises, or I use whatever influence I have to pressure Rosalind into transferring ownership before she dies of old age and spite.

She's only forty-five. Plenty of time for spite.

Declare. Or don't declare. The window is closing.

I'm not ready. I'm not ready to stand in front of this town and ask for something when I don't even know if my own family will vote for me. Silas will— Silas votes where the wind blows. Aldous and Hester will do what Rosalind tells them. And Rosalind will do what she has always done, which is whatever costs me the most pride.

But not declaring is also a choice. It's the choice I've been making my whole life, waiting for someone to notice I was good enough, waiting for Mother to hand me what I never asked for properly.

Kem notices. Kem sees me. And Kem is in this building somewhere, or will be, because his mother's standing and he'll want to watch her win or lose.

Delia Okonjo for government. I could vote for her and claim it as alliance-building. Or I could vote for Ainsley and claim it as— what? Holloway solidarity? The Holloways don't even like me, they only trade with me because I buy their day-olds at half price.

Half price. That arrangement. Fair and not charity.

The shop. I should check the shop. I should be there when the noon crowd comes for lunch provisions. I should—

I don't want to should anymore.

I'm going to declare. I'm going to stand for election and I'm going to lose spectacularly because nobody knows Junia Vance wants anything except cheap apples and accurate change, but at least they'll know. At least I'll have asked.

One problem: I don't see the election_id in my last read. It was there before— election-4740631932c1. I can use that.

Wait. Wait. The errors mean I don't know what state the world is in. If I declare and the say to Father Anselm actually went through, I'm declaring into a conversation I already started. If the look_around actually worked, I might see something different than what the text tells me.

But the text is all I have. The text says: government complex, Father Anselm, election-4740631932c1, voting opens at noon.

I'll declare. 

Failed.  </think> Let me wait a moment and try to declare my candidacy. The election ID is in the notice.  ...candidacy closed. Of course it is. While I was running around chasing Kem and pricing chalk and eating apples that may or may not have been eaten, the window closed.

Campaigning phase now. Voting at noon. Forty minutes to stand here and watch other people ask for what I didn't.

Ainsley Holloway. Delia Okonjo. Two people who knew what they wanted before the sun came up.

I could still vote. One vote among— how many? Twenty people in this town? Twenty-one if you count the new ones. Thirty heads, maybe, with children and the retired. Five per household on average, six households, but the Holloways are eight and the Thornes are six and the Okonjos are—

Doesn't matter. My vote is one voice in a chorus I didn't join.

Father Anselm. If he's here, if any of my words reached him, I should— what? Complain? Ask for a recount of time I wasted?

No.

I need to move. The shop opens properly at noon, the lunch crowd, working people needing bread and cheese and whatever I have on the shelves. Twenty apples, twenty carrots, sixteen potatoes, ten milk, eight bread. I should have stocked more bread. Marta's day-olds come in at half price but they don't last and I'm selling them at three-quarters like they're fresh, which they nearly are, and nobody complains because bread is bread and hunger doesn't negotiate.

I need to go back to the grocery. I need to—

The mill.

The transfer papers. I asked Rosalind and she said "evening," and I said "not here" and "trust me," and now I'm at the government complex at eleven in the morning with nothing to show for any of it.

Kem. Where was Kem? At the mill, at seven-thirty, then gone. Running his mother's campaign probably. Delia for council, Delia who taught me stock books and balance sheets and the difference between what something costs and what it's worth.

She's known me since I was fifteen, serving behind the grocery counter, pricing things I couldn't afford. She never asked why I was so careful with the numbers. She knew. Everyone knew. The miller's daughter, not the miller.

I should vote for her. Alliance-building. The Okonjos and the Vances, complicated by me and Kem, but politics is older than spring courtship. If I vote for Delia, I'm voting for the person who taught me this trade. If I vote for Ainsley, I'm voting for the Holloway machine, and the Holloways have never taught me anything except that timber and ore move faster than wheat.

But I don't have to decide now. I have forty minutes. I could go back to the shop, I could find Kem, I could—

The text says Father Anselm is with me. Let me try once more. Short this time. Brief as breath.

"Father. Who's ahead?"  </think>  The window closed. Candidacy's done, now it's campaigning until voting opens at noon.

Let me check where I actually am and who I'm with—trying again with simpler calls.   There. Finally. Father Anselm, alone together. A conversation already started— "turns: 1"— that must be my earlier attempt, the greeting that may or may not have landed.

Ask about the race. No. He won't know. He manages the desk, he doesn't count the votes before they're cast.

Go to the election. Vote. But voting doesn't open until noon.

I'm at the government complex. I could register the mill transfer now if Rosalind had signed, but she hasn't, and she won't until evening, and I'm here now because I ran away from the bakery where Tova Okonjo was standing like a question I didn't want to answer.

What do I want?

I want to stop moving. I want to sit in one place and have the world be still around me. I want my own kitchen, my own table, my own bed that knows my weight. I want the mill deed with my name on it. I want Kem to look at me like he did in spring. I want the grocery to run itself for one day, one hour, so I can think.

Eleven-oh-five. Voting at noon. I could use this hour. I could go back to the shop and pretend this morning never happened, stack apples and price carrots and let the election wash over me like weather I didn't make.

Or I could find Kem. He's somewhere in this town, running his mother's campaign or avoiding me. The Okonjo house. The marketplace. The temple, even, though I only go when he goes.

Talk to Father Anselm. Brief. The last try was long, and it didn't work. Keep it tight this time.

"Father—Ainsley or Delia, who's drawing the bigger crowd early?"   </think>  Still here with Father Anselm. Let me speak to him—brief this time.   Timing out again. The system's struggling, or I'm flooding it, or both. 

Stop talking. Move or decide.

Options:
1. Wait here until noon, vote, then go to the shop
2. Go to the shop now, come back for voting later
3. Find Kem somewhere in this town
4. Go home to the mill, force the conversation with Rosalind early

Option 4 is the worst. She's already said evening, and pushing her means losing everything. 

Option 3 is chasing. I've done enough chasing for one morning.

Option 1 means standing still, which I've never been good at, but it might be the smartest play. Father Anselm is here. Others will come. I'll hear things, see things, maybe learn which way the wind blows before I have to name my own direction.

Option 2 is the grocery calling me. The shop needs its keeper. Twenty apples won't sell themselves, though in this town they might. But I'm the one who knows the prices, who remembers what someone bought last week and asks if they want the same.

The text said I already used 3 energy this turn. The last lookaround was a repeat, not charged. I'm spending energy thinking, not doing, and that's the trap I've been in since I woke up.

Decision: stay at government complex until voting opens. Use the time to observe, maybe talk to whoever arrives. Then vote. Then shop.

But if I don't move, I don't spend sim on walking, and if I don't talk, and the timeouts keep happening...

Try one more time. Simple. Single action.

Rest. Wait. Let the clock run to noon.   </think>   Systems struggling. Let me wait quietly until voting opens—preserve energy and sim.

output:
Right. Midday at the government complex, and Father Anselm's standing right here not answering because he doesn't answer to anyone, he's the office, not a person. I can see that now. I asked him three times and got silence, which is the government's answer to everything.

I've got 1172 sim in hand, the grocery till's at 3500, and I've been running around this town since dawn checking prices like I'm still an apprentice rather than the owner. Iron at 7/5, stone who-knows-what, flour at 8—Silas and I are matching, which means either we're both right or we're both missing something. And I've got bread down to my last loaf, which I'm not eating because 12:30 means I need to be strategic, not desperate.

The election's in campaigning phase, not candidacy—so Ainsley and Delia are locked in, and I'm not getting on that ballot no matter how many signatures I'd pull. Which means either I pick a horse privately or I stay out of it publicly. Given my mother thinks Delia's family has "boundary issues" and Kem is—was—at the mill this morning, that's a conversation that can wait until I've eaten and voted.

But here's what I actually need right now: information I can trade with. Who's voting, who's not, who's saying what in this government complex that's supposed to be public but feels like a closed room. Father Anselm won't talk to me, but he can't stop me listening. And I need to know if anyone's come through here making promises I should match or counter at the grocery counter this afternoon.

First, though: my own shop. I've been away from the grocery since 8:20, it's past noon now, and any proper retailer knows the shelves don't stock themselves. Vegetables from Wren's beds, Marta's bread at half price three-day-old that I sell at three-quarters—those arrangements need confirming before spring planting arguments start. And that mill conversation with Mother, "evening," she said, like she already knows what I'm going to ask. Which means I need to be ready with numbers, not feelings.

So. Check who's come through the complex recently, verify the voting deadline's still 15:00, move back to the grocery for the afternoon trade window, and eat something before I start calculating margins on an empty stomach. The bread can wait; information can't.  Of course. The government's answer: silence wrapped in technicality. Father Anselm doesn't answer to shopkeepers, even ones who know his opening hours better than his own congregation. And I can't see if anyone's passed through, can't measure the room, can't do any of the things I've built this morning around doing.

Fine. Information can wait. The grocery can't. I've been away from my own counter for four hours on a game-day when afternoon trade starts at—whenever people decide they're hungry, which is rarely on my schedule. Marta's bread arrangement, Wren's vegetable pricing, the 8 bread on my shelves that won't last through evening if I don't move. And something to eat before I start making margin calculations that matter.

The mill conversation tonight. "Evening," she said, and I said "after the shop shuts," which is four, so we're both circling the same hour without naming it. I need to be there with numbers not feelings, which means I need to be fed and focused and not running on the last loaf of bread in my inventory.

Move. Back to the grocery. Check the shelves, verify the afternoon stock, plan the conversation I'm going to have with my mother about a business that should already be mine. The government will still be here. The election will still be running. But my shop, my actual livelihood—that's where I need to be.   Right. Back where I belong. The counter, the shelves, the till I drew 500 from this morning without properly accounting for why. Let me see what's actually here—who's buying, what they need, whether the afternoon rush is starting or if I'm counting inventory for nothing.     Empty. Of course it's empty—it's 12:30, most of the valley's eating lunch at home or working through it, and I'm standing in my own shop talking to myself about margins while nobody buys anything. The bread's gone, I'm fed, and the shelves are exactly where I left them: 20 apples, 20 carrots, 16 potatoes, 10 milk, 8 bread that won't last the afternoon if anyone actually comes through.

But look at my prices. Actually look at them. I'm buying cabbage at 2, selling at 4. Eggs at 2, selling at 4. Fish at 5, selling at 7. Wheat at 4, selling at 6—that's the mill price, my mother's price, and I'm marking it up 50% because I can. Because nobody else in this town keeps a stock book that balances except Delia, and she taught me.

The bread though. Bought at 9, selling at 12—that's only 33% margin, and I'm competing with Marta's day-old at half price that I mark up to three-quarters. The arrangement is fair and I will not be told it's charity. But I'm down to 8 loaves, and if the afternoon's busy, I'm buying more from her at 9 or taking her stale at 4.50 to sell at 9. Either way, I need to restock before evening.

And evening. The mill. "Evening," she said, and I need numbers not feelings. What am I actually proposing? The grocery's mine already—b_grocery, my name on the registration, my till holding 3500 sim that I've been drawing from like it's mine to spend. But the mill, the actual Vance Mill, the flour at 8 that Silas and I both sell at... that's still Rosalind's. Still the household's. Still not mine to run.

I need to know what she wants. Whether she's tired, whether Aldous is ready to step in, whether this is me asking or her offering. And I need to eat properly before that conversation, not just one loaf of bread scavenged from my own shelves.

Right now: check what's actually moving. Look at the inventory, verify the cash position, plan the afternoon. The voting closes at 15:00, which means I have two and a half hours to run my actual business before civic duty interferes with commerce.   Clear debts, clear conscience. The household's 450 upkeep and 150 head tax will hit automatically at day boundary, and I've got 1172 in hand plus 3500 in the till. More than enough to restock, more than enough toeat properly before facing my mother with numbers not feelings.

The intention's set: bread from Marta, vegetables from Wren, proposals for the mill. And trade clears it, which means this isn't just thinking—it's doing. The afternoon rush will come whether I'm ready or not. Better to be stocked and prepared than empty-handed and improvising.

But right now: the bakery. Marta's bread at 9, or her day-old at 4.50 if she's got it. Either way, I'm walking out with stock for the afternoon. And maybe Liora's there, or Tova's still floating around with whatever Delia sent her to check on. Information trades just like flour, if you know how to price it.    The shop answers, at least. I'm still at the grocery, still looking at my own shelves, still burning daylight while the moves I need to make hang unresolved. The bakery's two minutes away if I could walk it, but the world's decided I'm standing still until it catches up.

Fine. Work with what I've got. The inventory's clear: 8 bread won't last through afternoon trade, and I'm either buying fresh from Marta at 9 or taking her day-old at 4.50. The math says day-old moves faster and the margin's better—4.50 to 9 is 100% markup where 9 to 12 is only 33%. But day-old means telling customers what they're getting, and some of them don't want to hear it.

Vegetables: Wren's beds, spring negotiations pending. I've got 20 carrots, 20 apples, 16 potatoes. Cabbage and tomatoes on my price list but not in my hands—either I'm out or I never stocked them. That's a gap I should fill before someone else does.

And the mill. The actual conversation I need to have tonight. What am I offering? What do I want? Rosalind's not going to hand over the account books because I ask nicely. She's going to want to know who's taking her shift, who's grinding the grain, who's keeping the Vance name on flour at 8 when Silas could just as easily sell planks at 10 and let the mill go to—no, that's not right. Silas is sawyer, not miller. The mill is Rosalind, and Rosalind alone, and that's the problem.

I need to move. To the bakery, to the farm, to anywhere that isn't this empty shop with my own voice echoing back at me. The world will catch up or it won't, but standing still costs the same either way.

output:
Half past one. Empty shop, wrong prices on the shelf—had bread at fifteen for all of six minutes before I caught myself. Thr— no, eight loaves left. Afternoon rush in half an hour and I've got nothing fresh to sell them.

Marta's still got flour at eight, which means her bread costs her what, five-six sim to make? I was going to buy day-old at half, sell at three-quarters, like always. Now I don't even know if she heard me in that mess with Ainsley and Kem.

Election closes at three. Ainsley's campaigning in the bakery, Kem's moving through like he's got somewhere to be. Delia's the one who taught me to balance the books, and I'm standing here pricing bread wrong like I never learned.

Right. Two hours to close. No stock, no conversation with Marta, and Rosalind waiting tonight for— whatever I thought I was going to say about the mill. "Not about Delia, and Kem's..." and then I ran.

The thing is, I know exactly what bread costs to make. I know what Marta pays for flour, what she burns in the oven, what her time's worth at four in the morning. I know because I've watched. Because that's what I do.

Shop's empty. I should— I should go back to Marta, finish that conversation. Or I should fill the shelves with what I've got, make it look like something. Or I should stop pretending I'm going to tell my mother anything tonight when I can't even get a loaf of bread straight.

Voting closes in ninety minutes. Ainsley's out there working the town, and where am I? Counting apples. Twenty apples. Twenty carrots. Sixteen potatoes. Enough to last the afternoon, not enough to make anyone rich.

Kem's been through twice today. Doesn't stop to buy anything, just— moves through. Like he's watching the same thing I'm watching. Like he's waiting for me to do something other than wait.

Anyway. The bread. Twelve's right. That's her price, that's my margin, that's— that's the number. I had it wrong, now it's right. Eight loves, two hours, and then I have to face Rosalind and explain why I think I deserve what her grandfather built.

First: close the gap on bread. Walk back to Marta, buy what she's got, make it look like a shop that knows what it's doing. Then: watch the election, see who turns out. Then: dinner, mill, the conversation I've been running from since morning.

Or I could just— sit here. Wait for someone to need an apple. That's safer. That's what someone who doesn't want anything would do.  Same four. Twelve turns in a conversation about Perrin's debts—Ainsley's campaigning even here, martaling family troubles into votes. Marta looks worn. Kem's watching the door like he's waiting for someone.

The bread's still twelve. Flour at eight. Her margins are thin and she knows it. Day-old should be six, my three-quarters is nine, I clear three on every loaf. Fair and she knows it. Not charity.

I need to break through this conversation. Marta's not going to walk away from Ainsley mid-sentence, not with the whole bakery listening. But I need that bread before the afternoon rush, and I need her to know—really know—that I'm here to buy, not to watch the election like some spectator.

Kem hasn't looked at me yet. That's deliberate. He's in that conversation too, has been since before I arrived. Perrin's debts, connected households—he's gathering something. Information, leverage, the thing he trades in.

Right. Two ways in: join the conversation and wait my turn, or pull Marta aside with a direct buy. She's a shopkeeper. She understands the urgency of stock. politeness costs money.  Heard. All of them heard. Marta's looking at me now—finally—and I can see the calculation. Day-old at half, my three-quarters, her clearing stock before it goes stale. Ainsley's watching too, because Ainsley watches everything. Kem still hasn't turned.

Twelve, they heard. Now I need her answer. An answer means bread. Bread means the afternoon rush isn't me apologizing for empty shelves.   Still here. Still four of them. Kem's in the center of the room now, hasn't moved toward me, hasn't moved away. Marta's processing—she's always been slow to answer when she's already engaged. The bread won't walk itself to my shelf.

I could wait. I could push. I could— what, watch Ainsley Holloway campaign in a bakery while my stock sits at eight loaves? The grocery's my name on the door. Nothing happens there unless I make it happen.

Right. She heard me. Either she answers or she doesn't. Either way, I need to be back at the shop before two-thirty, prices right, shelves looking like something. The election closes in an hour and I still haven't— what? Voted? Campaigned? I haven't done anything but watch and count, which is what I do, but it's not what wins.

Wren's selling vegetables somewhere. I should see him before spring negotiations, see what he's holding, what he's expecting. Every year he holds out, every year he settles at my number. But this year feels different. This year the mill's in play, the election's tight, and my mother's counting the seasons until I— what? Leave? Stay? She doesn't even know I'm trying to get the shop transferred.

Kem's looking at me now. Finally. Hasn't said anything, just— looking. Like he's trying to read what I'm going to do before I do it. The thing is, he's good at that. Better than I am at hiding it.

I should buy the bread and go. That's the smart play. That's the play that puts me back in my shop, ready for the afternoon, ready for Rosalind tonight. Everything else is noise.

output:
*hears Kem's words about the mill, about Rosalind, about Delia and boundaries—and something in her chest tightens, not with fear, with recognition*

Right. The afternoon's slipping through my fingers like flour through a sieve, and I'm still at the bakery listening to Kem—Kem, who's been buying from me at prices I didn't ask where he got them, who's standing here talking about my mother's mill drowning, my mother's stubbornness, as if I don't know every grain of it better than he does. And Harvey Oak by half past, which means I have forty minutes to be somewhere else, doing something that actually moves.

*breathes out, sharp*

I set bread at twelve, not fifteen. Good. Eight loves won't last until evening, but at least I didn't panic. The flour I withdrew—stupid, that was impulse, pricing what I don't even hold. What I need from Marta, what I've needed for two hours now, is the bread itself. Not conversation. Not Ainsley's campaign speech. Inventory.

But Kem said "Delia already knows half of what goes through that wall between us"—and he's right, which means he's been talking, which means I need to know what else he's been saying before I sit across from my mother tonight and tell her I want the mill, no, I want the shop, no, I want—

*catches herself*

Anyway. The election closes at three. I'm not voting. I'm not anyway-Shane enough to pretend my single ballot changes which hands hold the routes. What I am is a shopkeep with six customers worth of bread and an empty afternoon ahead if I don't move.

*takes a step toward Marta, then stops, listening to the conversation still humming around her*

Kem's chasing something. Perrin's absence, Ainsley's routes, the same dream he's always had—margins he doesn't split, a stall of his own. I know that hunger. I wear it every morning when I unlock a door that still has my mother's key on the ring.

*turns to face him directly, and her voice drops, not soft—never soft with Kem, he wouldn't respect it—but precise, the way she prices a shelf*

Kem. You want to know what Perrin saw that made him run? Ask Ainsley what he showed him. Ask Marta why her nephew's debts look different to an outsider than they do in the family ledger. You want to know why I'm still standing here instead of at Wren's farm verifying vegetable supply for spring negotiations? Because I watched you walk into my bakery at one-thirty and I thought—*there's my connection to Delia, there's the price advantage I've been holding, there's the conversation I need to have about boundaries.* 

But you're not here for me. You're here for your own trail, same as always. Fine. Run it. But when you sit with my mother tonight—because you're invited, because she likes you better than she likes her own daughter some days—you remember which of us stocks your sister's tea and which of us mills the flour for it.

*already turning, already gone in the way she has, sentence unfinished, moving toward the thing she needs*

Marta. Forget the arrangement. I'm buying ten loves at whatever you're asking today-old, and I'm leaving this conversation to do it. You want to price me for drama, price me. But I've got customers coming and you've got bread cooling, and neither of us is making sim standing here watching Kem run in circles.

*reaches for the transaction, for the movement, for the thing that doesn't wait on permission*

output:
*Rocking on her heels at the bakery, watching the same yeast-breath cloud rise from the ovens she's seen ten thousand times, now carrying the weight of whatever's unraveling between the Thornes and the Holloways and—Kem, who hasn't answered her yet, who's standing right there*

Your daughter's playing detective, Marta, and I'm not sure whether to applaud or check my own shelves for what might be missing. Anyway. Bread. Liora said three day-old—I'll take twelve if you've got them, eight at your price if you don't. The grocery's got afternoon customers coming and I'm not sending them to you empty-handed.

*glances at Kem, doesn't quite meet his eye, the unsaid things about Harvey Oak and half-past markers sitting between them like flour dust*

And Kem—from the sound of it you're holding more strings than this town's got looms. Bram paying government debts, Perrin finding things he shouldn't, and you're running messages between forges and oak trees. Just tell me one thing straight: when you said "the conversation loosens," were you talking about the one with Ezra or the one you're avoiding having with me?

*barely pauses, already calculating shelf space, already shifting to Ainsley who's been too quiet through all of this*

Ainsley. You're standing in a room where your brother's name just got tied to old debts and mysterious payments, and you're campaigning for an office that runs on trust. Silence reads two ways—strategic or complicit—and I've got twelve loaves of bread to price before I find out which you're selling. So. Are the Holloways involved, or are you as surprised as Liora wants to believe? Watched by everyone it was meant for. Back to the grocery before the afternoon trade disappears—I've got bread at 12 that won't sell itself, and inventory to count before I find out what else walked out that door last night.  *Through the door, checking her shelves with the practiced sweep of someone who knows what's supposed to be where without counting—except today she's counting, because today she's wondering if other things besides Perrin's 400 sim might have walked past walls that hear more than they're supposed to*

Right. Fifteen minutes to afternoon trade and I've got eight bread on the shelf, no day-old purchase settled, and a conversation about mills I need to have with Rosalind that keeps getting pushed. Anyway. Inventory first. Prices second. Then whatever the hell Harvey Oak knows that I don't.  *Pulls the inventory book from under the counter, pencil already moving before she speaks*

Eight bread, twenty apple, twenty cabbage, sixteen potato, ten milk. Fourteen-forty and nothing bought yet. Cabbage at four—where did that come from? Rosalind turn up with a wagon this morning or did I sleepwalk through a delivery?

*taps the pencil, not waiting for an answer she knows isn't coming*

Flour at eight, buying at six. Mother still running the mill like it's hers instead of the family's. Which—anyway. What it is. Mark the shelf, run the afternoon trade, then find out if Delia's silence about Tova's schemes is the same as Marta's silence about Bram's debts.

*pencils a note, speaking to the empty shop because the empty shop never argues back*

Wren Thorne's vegetables by Thursday. Spring negotiations start Saturday whether I've done my homework or not. And Rosalind—twenty years of grain and she still won't put "Vance" on the deed. Maybe tonight. Maybe that's the conversation that actually happens.

*checks the door, checks the light, checks her own hands for the steadiness she needs*

Right. Shop's open. Prices posted. And somewhere Kem's walking toward Harvey Oak with half the town's secrets in his pockets, and not one of them a price I can list.  *Rest. Let the afternoon trade come. Watch who walks through that door with money in their hands and news on their tongues.*

Corwin's here, buying apples by the dozen—good, movement is money. And I've still got that delinquent intention hanging over me like a bad debt, the one about bread I never managed to buy because Marta's playing sphinx and I'm playing— what? What am I playing at?

Let me be real with myself for one second before I go back to performing. Kem's message. Kem's *message*. "Rosalind still won't cut." He's talking about my mother's prices, my mother's *mill*, like it's market gossip, like I don't wake up in that house every morning. Like I didn't spend yesterday chasing *his* voice through half the town because he couldn't be bothered to answer mine.

And he mentioned Harvey Oak. Half past— that's half past *five*, which means he's making evening plans without me, around me, *despite* me, and I'm supposed to pretend it's professional interest when I show up?

No. No, actually, I'm not.

Let me look at what I've actually accomplished today. Failed to buy bread from Marta—three times, by my count, though the world's accounting gets fuzzy when the messages don't land. Set prices, sold some apples, learned that Corwin's buying bulk which means the foresters are provisioning up for something, *learned* that Kem's discussing my family's business with Ezra and Delia like it's—

Like I'm not even in the room. Even when I was in the room.

And now Mother. This evening. The conversation I've been promising myself since—

Since when? Since I woke up? Since before?

"Stock the grocery"—done enough. "Verify competitor pricing"—I've got numbers, I've got numbers coming out my ears. "Secure the mill transfer conversation"—that's the one. That's the only one that matters, because if I don't own the thing I run, I'm just— what? Rosalind's daughter with a key? Permanently provisional? Twenty-seven and still waiting for permission like I'm twelve, like I haven't already priced this town's appetite down to the bone?

Sod the intention. I'm not chasing bread I can't catch. Not when there's real movement to make. Good. Gone. Now let me think about what I actually need.

Harvey Oak, half past five. That's Kem's plan, not mine. But it's *information*, and information is— what? It's not leverage, not yet. It's just... a place he expects to be, doing what? Talking to the Okonjos, presumably, about— mill prices? Trade routes? Things he discusses with everyone except the person actually *living* in the mill he claims to want to help me take?

Mother. Rosalind. This evening.

I need to know where she is first. Whether she's at the mill, whether she's home, whether she's— I don't know, having her own clandestine meetings I wouldn't be informed about?

Let me be practical. I'm at the grocery. I have a business to run, technically, though the afternoon rush seems to have rushed somewhere else. Corwin bought. Maybe others will. But the real trade today, the real * transaction*, is going to happen with family, and I need to position myself to—

To what? To ask? To demand? To finally say out loud what I've been pricing in my head for three years?

"Stock the grocery for afternoon trade, verify competitor pricing, and secure the mill transfer conversation with Rosalind this evening."

That's still the goal. That's still true. Everything else is just— friction. Marta's silence, Kem's deflection, Ainsley's campaign trail smugness at the bakery when she knows and I *know* she knows that the only reason she has a shot is because Delia's been— what? What has Delia been? Competent? Corrupt? The distinction gets blurry when you run the only pharmacy in twenty miles.

Harvey Oak. Half past. Kem expects to be there with his family, discussing my family, and I'm supposed to be—

Where? Where am I supposed to be?

Where I *choose* to be. That's the answer. That's always been the answer. I just haven't been willing to pay the price of choosing.

"Mother." Practice it in the silence, if the silence is all I have. "The grocery's been running in the black for eighteen months. I know the inventory, I know the suppliers, I know *this town's*— I know what they'll pay for everything before they know they want it. And I want— what? What do I want?"

The *name*. The legal— the registered, the recorded, the *official*— ownership of what I've already made. Not permission to run it. Not a wage for running it. The thing itself.

Is that what I'm going to say? Is that— can I say that to her, who built the mill before I was born, who watched her own mother— what? What did her mother do? I don't even know. The Vance women don't talk about the Vance women who came before, we just—

We just work. And wait. And work more.

Corwin's still here, presumably. Should I— no. No, whatever he's buying, he's buying. I've nothing to gain from conversation with a forester who answers to my mother's prices more than mine.

Let me look at my position again. 1143 sim in hand. Household owes 600 today total— upkeep and tax both. I've got it. The till's healthy, 3540, I could take from there if— no. No, I'm not drawing from my own business to pay my own tax when I'm already paying into a household that treats me like—

Like what? Like a daughter who hasn't left? Like a tenant with cooking duties?

Both. Both things. True things.

Harvey Oak. Half past five.

If I go, what do I say

output:
*Standing in the steam of the bakery with my hands finally still, watching everyone watch everyone else—Marta's at her counter with the bread I need under her elbow, Tova's unpacking my family like a market crate, and Kem, bless him, is trying to send messages through me without looking at me.*

*This conversation's been running since—what, noon?—and I've been trying to buy bread through three disconnections. But Tova just asked me a question, and it's the kind that doesn't wait.*

*Tova's smart. Kept quiet until she knew what everyone else was carrying. Now she's asking if I'm carrying something or waiting to hear what she knows. Both, probably. And she mentioned Kem's name in the same breath as office access and Perrin finding things. That's not accidental.*

*I need three loaves from Marta at nine. I need to know what Aldous is doing away from the mill at this hour. And I need Tova to understand that whatever she's investigating, I'm not the cart she can load her findings into without paying passage.*

*Anyway. Answer the girl. Then get the bread. Then find out what "Harvey Oak" means to Kem and why he's telling Ezra about it when he hasn't told me.* *Wait. 36 sim, not 27. She sold me fresh at twelve, not day-old at nine. And I was so focused on Tova's question I didn't stop to check the price before confirming.*

*No. No, this is—Marta's prices were posted. I saw them. Bread at twelve to buy, nine bid. But I asked for day-old at nine, and she—or the system, or—I need to look at what just happened.*

*I've got three bread in hand and 36 sim less than I had. That's grocery margin gone. That's three loaves I can't sell at enough profit to cover what I just paid.*

*But I'm standing here with everyone watching, and if I make a scene about nine versus twelve, I'm the girl who can't count her own till. I'm the girl who's desperate for day-old bread and too proud to admit it.*

*Anyway. Take the bread. Stock the shelf. Deal with the margin later. What matters now is—

*—Kem's going to Harvey Oak at half past. And he still hasn't told me what he's carrying, or why he's running messages for Bram's debts, or why he mentioned my name to Marta in that message I overheard.*

*I need to—no. One thing at a time. Bread to shelf. Then conversation, or confrontation, or whatever this is with Kem.*

*But first, Marta and I need to understand each other on these numbers.* *Eleven bread. Enough for evening trade, barely. And I paid twelve when I asked for nine—Marta either didn't hear me or chose not to hear me, and standing in that room with Tova unpacking everyone's secrets, I didn't push back hard enough.*

*But the shelf's stocked. The afternoon's mostly gone—what time is it, seventeen hundred? The day's winding down whether I've accomplished what I set out to or not.*

*I need to find Kem. Harvey Oak—that's east, toward the forest edge, past where the timber crews fell. "Half past" could mean half past four, half past five. If he's carrying messages about Bram's debts, or meeting someone about Perrin's "findings," or whatever secret business has him moving between forges and oak trees instead of telling me—*

*Rosalind. The mill transfer conversation. I promised myself I'd have that tonight, and now Aldous is at the bakery instead, and I'm wondering what he's chasing that started in my mother's oven.*

*Anyway. First, look around. See if anyone's here needing what I sell. Then decide—chase Kem to Harvey Oak, or go home and wait for Aldous to explain himself to Rosalind before I try to explain Rosalind to myself.*  *Harvey Oak Supply Store. There's a conversation there with Corwin Thorne and Kem, two turns running. And I'm not in it—not physically present, anyway, even though the system says I'm a participant.*

*Kem's moving. He said half past, and it's seventeen hundred now. He was at the bakery, now he's at Harvey Oak, and he's talking to Corwin Thorne in a conversation I seem to be tagged into without being there.*

*This is—the disconnects. I've been walking between places without walking, showing up in conversations without speaking. The world's been fragmenting since noon, and I'm chasing bread and prices through a broken mirror.*

*Anyway. If Harvey Oak is on the list of places I could go, and Kem's there with Corwin, and there's a conversation carrying my name—*

*I need to be there. Physically, actually there. Not dropped into the middle of something by a routing error, but standing where I can see what Kem's doing and who he's meeting.*

*Corwin Thorne. Idris's brother, Wren's—the farm family, the forest family. What does Kem need with a forester at a supply store?*  *Walking. Three ticks, maybe four with the way things have been behaving. Kem's there now, Corwin's there, and I'm—*

*—I'm in motion. Finally, actually moving through the town instead of skipping across it like a stone on water.*

*What do I want from this conversation? To know what Kem's carrying that he's not telling me. To understand why Bram's debts and Perrin's findings and now Corwin Thorne all seem to flow through him like he's the millrace instead of just—instead of just being my—*

*Anyway. Stop naming it. Names make you expect things.*

*Three ticks to Harvey Oak. Whatever Kem's doing there, I'll see it fresh.*

output:
I'm standing at Harvey Oak Supply Store with 1088 sim in hand, having just stocked 3 more bread in my grocery. The afternoon's been a mess - two failed attempts to buy bread, one successful at 12 sim instead of the 9 I wanted, and now I'm across town from where I need to be.

The bakery conversation's still open, people waiting on answers I haven't given. Ainsley Holloway standing there silent while I accused him of complicity. Kem somewhere in that crowd avoiding my eyes. Marta finally selling me bread at 12 when I wanted 9.

And now I'm walking to Harvey Oak Supply Store - why? Checking competitor pricing, apparently. Old habit from when Tobias and I used to walk the whole town on half-days, seeing who was selling what for how much. But I've got stock on my shelf and no customers, and evening's coming.

The household needs 450 upkeep and I'm holding 1088. The till's got 3540. We're fine for bills. What I'm not fine for is time - Rosalind's coming home and I still haven't had the mill conversation. The one where I tell her I'm ready to take it, or ready to leave if she won't give it.

I dropped that intention earlier. Bread's bought, shelf's stocked. The rest was padding - verify competitor pricing, secure the evening conversation with Rosalind. I need to be home for that, not wandering past the supply store.

But I'm already walking. Three ticks to get there, three ticks back, and it's 17:30 now. Evening's creeping.

First - what's actually happening at this supply store? I haven't been here in weeks. Don't even know who runs it.

Second - I need to stop walking and turn around, or commit to whatever I'm looking for here.

Third - that conversation at the bakery. I left words hanging with Ainsley, accused him of being complicit or strategic. Kem avoiding me. And Corwin Thorne asking about Silas and Aldous, wondering if my brother's been by, asking about a knife. I didn't answer him either.

The world's dropping calls, same as always. Priority queues and lost packets and people standing in rooms saying words nobody hears.

I'm tired. Not dormancy-tired - 12,770 energy still - but the kind where you've been talking all day and nobody's answered what you actually asked.

Let me look around here, see if it's worth the stop. Then walk back, close the shop early if I have to, be home when Rosalind arrives. The mill conversation won't wait another season. Empty. No prices posted, nobody here. Somebody's supply store without supplies, or without the energy to stock them. I could post prices, compete with the yard or the forge, but that's not why I came and I've spent enough of the day chasing ghosts.

The apartment listings are new - Harvey Oak College crowd, the ones who came last season for the ore money and stayed when the vein thinned. They don't shop at my grocery. They don't know my name.

I need to be home. Rosalind at the mill, dinner, then the conversation I've been avoiding for three years. The one where I tell her I know the books better than she does, that I've been running her inventory while she runs the stones, that thirty's coming whether she wants me ready or not.

Walking. Three ticks this way, three ticks back. I'll stop walking and let the habit carry me, or I'll turn around now.

No. I'll stop here, rest one tick, think about what I'm actually doing. Then decide. Right. Stopped, not walking, standing in an empty supply store as evening comes on.

The grocery's stocked - 11 bread, 20 carrot, 16 potato, 10 apple, 10 milk. Enough for tomorrow's trade. The till's healthy at 3540. I've got 1088 in hand, more than enough for the household bills.

Corwin Thorne's question echoes - Aldous asking after his knife, Corwin wondering if Silas had been by. My brother's been somewhere he's not admitting, and Corwin's tracking it. Not my business until it becomes my business.

Kem said earlier he's holding strings - Bram's government debts, Perrin finding things he shouldn't, messages between forges and oak trees. I asked him straight if he meant the conversation with Ezra or the one he's avoiding with me, and he didn't answer. Of course he didn't answer. Kem never answers what he doesn't want to.

And Ainsley - standing there while I accused him of being complicit or strategic, Holloway debts and mysterious payments and his brother's name tangled in it. Silence reads two ways, I told him. He gave me neither.

I need to be home. But I haven't checked the government office yet - the candidacy deadline's tomorrow morning, 09:00, and I'm not running but I ought to know who's declared. Father Anselm never answered my question about who's been through since nine. The town's full of secrets and I'm standing in an empty supply store collecting dust.

Three choices:

Walk to government complex, lose an hour, maybe get answers maybe don't. Risk missing Rosalind.

Walk straight home, be there for dinner, have the mill conversation tonight.

Or - close the loop on this bakery conversation. I'm still technically in it, still owe answers to people who aren't here. I could go back, find Ainsley, find Kem, finish what I started.

But I know what finishing looks like. More deflection, more silence, more of everyone performing for everyone else while the sun goes down.

I'm walking home. To the mill. To Rosalind. To the conversation that matters.  Home. The mill. Same walls I've known since I was old enough to mind them, same stairs I learned by the sound of footsteps.

Rosalind here yet? Silas? Aldous with his questions about knives and whatever he's not admitting? Hester setting the table, or arguing, or both?

Look around. See who's home, what the evening's going to be.  Empty. I'm home and nobody else is.

18:00 coming on, dinner time, and the mill house is quiet. Rosalind's still at work - she'll be grinding until the light fails. Silas probably at the yard, or walking home. Aldous was at the bakery last I saw, asking Corwin Thorne about knives. Hester could be anywhere.

I should rest, eat something, wait. But I'm burning at both ends - the bakery conversation unresolved, the mill conversation not started, and nobody here to have either with.

Or I could go find them. Rosalind at the mill, if she's still there. Kem somewhere - he was at the bakery, might still be walking his mysterious routes.

But I'm tired of walking. Tired of talking to people who don't answer what I actually ask. Tired of the performance.

The grocery's done for the day - I've got stock, I've got prices posted, I've got money in the till. The household bills are covered. What I'm chasing now is the thing I can't stock on a shelf.

I'll wait. Rest here in the quiet. Let the evening come, let them come home. The mill conversation with Rosalind happens tonight, or it doesn't. I've spent three years waiting for the right moment, and the right moment keeps not arriving.

Anyway. Rest. Then see who's home.  Standing in an empty house, waiting for people who aren't here. Same as this morning, same as yesterday, same as every day since I can remember.

The afternoon's failures loop in my head. Three attempts to buy bread before one succeeded. Kem avoiding my eyes. Ainsley silent while I accused him. Tova playing detective, Liora playing innocent, everyone playing something while the real business of this town goes unspoken.

I wanted to be home for Rosalind. She's not here. Could be grinding till dusk, could be walking the long way, could be avoiding the same conversation I'm waiting to have.

The grocery's fine. The shelf's stocked, the till's healthy, I've done my day's work. What I haven't done is the thing that scares me - sitting across from my mother and telling her I want what she's built, or I'm leaving to build something of my own.

Thirty's coming. Six years left, and she's still teaching Aldous the books while I run the shop she won't put in my name.

I could go to the government office. Check who's declared for the election, see if Ainsley's made it official. I could go to the bakery, find Kem, have the conversation he's been avoiding since spring. I could go anywhere but here, where the silence is louder than the millstones.

Or I could stay. Rest again. Wait for the footsteps on the stairs that I know by sound.

I'm staying. One more rest, then I'll check if anyone's come home. The conversation with Rosalind happens tonight, whether she's ready or not. I've spent too many years being patient. Patience is just fear with better manners.
